practicalQuestion: What training qualities and dose constraints should guide a low-volume strength-and-power session 48 hours before competition when the goal is to preserve readiness without creating unnecessary fatigue?

decisionContext.outcome: Retain a meaningful performance stimulus while limiting residual fatigue
decisionContext.constraints: Thirty-minute session; existing sport practice; no athlete-specific medical restrictions

evidenceConfidence.rationale: No source in the pack tests a strength-and-power session placed 48 hours before competition. The relevant evidence is indirect. It covers how long a high-volume sprint session depresses speed and strength, how set structure changes acute fatigue, which power methods may suit short in-season sessions, and what practitioners report doing. Each piece transfers only partly to collegiate team-sport athletes, so options are presented without a single recommended direction.

dimensions.sourceReview: Five full-text screened sources were used: one meta-analysis, one systematic review, one case series, and one qualitative interview study. One legacy record not full-text reviewed was used only for monitoring. Warm-up, preseason, caffeine, heat, longitudinal testing, and practice-design sources were set aside as not addressing the question.
dimensions.directness: Low. No source manipulates session content or dose 48 hours before competition and measures competition readiness. The sprint study gives the closest timing signal, but it describes a high-volume session, not a low-volume one.
dimensions.consistency: No material disagreement. The sources point the same general way: high-volume maximal work can leave fatigue for 48 hours or more, and lower-fatigue set structures and lighter, velocity-focused methods are favored for short sessions. They answer different sub-questions, so agreement is loose rather than tested.
dimensions.transferability: Partial. Populations were male amateur soccer players (sprint study), mixed meta-analysed resistance training samples, team-sport athletes in a power-training review, 12 applied practitioners, and 18 elite male football players. None are collegiate multi-sport samples and female athletes are not represented in the cited excerpts.

bottomLine.text: The library does not directly test what a session 48 hours before competition should contain. Indirect evidence suggests that high-volume maximal efforts can depress speed and posterior chain strength for 48 to 72 hours. Set structures that spread rest, and lighter loads moved fast, are reported to limit acute fatigue or suit short sessions. Treat these as options to weigh, not a tested prescription.

actions.title: Option: keep maximal-intent volume low
actions.text: A high-volume maximal sprinting session reduced sprint performance and posterior chain strength for 48 and 72 hours in amateur soccer players. That suggests avoiding high-volume maximal work in this window. The evidence does not test what lower volume is safe; the exact dose is professional judgment.

actions.title: Option: use cluster or rest-redistribution sets
actions.text: Across 32 studies, cluster and rest-redistribution set structures preserved velocity and power and reduced their decline during and after resistance training compared with traditional sets. This could help keep output high while limiting acute fatigue. The evidence measured acute effects, not readiness 48 hours later.

actions.title: Option: favor lighter loads moved at high velocity
actions.text: A review in team-sport athletes suggests optimal-load and velocity-based methods may suit shorter sessions with less time under tension while maximizing power and velocity, and that lighter, faster loading may benefit in-season periods. This fits a 30-minute session, but the review addresses longer-term power development, not pre-competition timing.

actions.title: Option: micro-dose or use isometric work
actions.text: Applied practitioners reported micro-dosing the resistance stimulus and using isometric exercise during fixture congestion. This is reported practice, not a tested outcome. The evidence does not show it preserves readiness better than other options.

monitoring.label: Countermovement jump with FT:CT
monitoring.text: In elite football players after matches, the flight time to contraction time ratio detected reduced recovery longer than jump height did. If staff already jump-test, FT:CT may be more informative than height alone. The evidence comes from post-match recovery, not pre-competition sessions.

monitoring.label: Within-session velocity or power drop
monitoring.text: Set structures that limited velocity and power decline were also linked to less fatigue after training. The evidence does not test a stopping threshold; watching for falling bar speed or power is a sensible caution, not a validated rule.

guardrails.text: Count the session against the full weekly load. Recovery after matches may take up to 72 hours or more in many team sports, and existing practice volume can make maintaining power and speed harder.
Do not treat this window as a place to add high-volume maximal sprinting. Decrements after such a session lasted at least 48 hours in the one study that measured them.

limitations.text: The 48 to 72 hour decrements come from 15 male amateur soccer players after a high-volume sprint session. They may not apply to low-volume work or to collegiate athletes in other sports.
The set-structure meta-analysis reports acute effects during and right after training, not readiness two days later.
Practitioner strategies come from interviews with 12 practitioners and describe what is done, not what works.

whatCouldChange.text: Data showing how long residual fatigue lasts after low-volume, cluster-structured, or velocity-based sessions would test whether the acute benefits carry to 48 hours.
Evidence in collegiate and female team-sport athletes would improve transferability.

claims.text: In 15 active male amateur soccer players, a high-volume maximal sprinting session significantly reduced theoretical maximal horizontal velocity and sprint performance for 48 and 72 hours afterward.

evidence.excerpt: Fifteen active male amateur soccer players participated. Changes in sprint performance-related factors and HSI risk factors were examined for 72 hours after high-volume MSS efforts (H-VMSSE)
Significant reductions in theoretical maximal horizontal velocity (P < 0.01; effect size [ES], -0.71) and performance (P = 0.02; ES, -0.59) were observed for 48 and 72 hours after H-VMSSE.

claims.text: In the same amateur soccer players, small but significant reductions in posterior chain force-generating capacity were detected 48 and 72 hours after the high-volume sprint session in both legs.

evidence.excerpt: Small but significant reductions in posterior chain muscle force-generating capacity were detected for 48 and 72 hours after H-VMSSE for the nondominant (P < 0.03; ES, -0.60) and dominant (P < 0.04; ES, -0.40) leg.

claims.text: A meta-analysis of 32 studies found that alternative set structures (cluster and rest redistribution) allowed greater velocity and power and mitigated declines in velocity and power during and after resistance training compared with traditional sets.

evidence.excerpt: Thirty-two studies were included. Pooled results revealed that alternative set structures allowed for greater absolute mean [standardized mean difference (SMD) = 0.60] and peak velocity (SMD = 0.41)
In addition, alternative set structures were also highly effective at mitigating a decline in velocity and power variables during (SMD = 0.83-1.97) and after RT (SMD = 0.58)

claims.text: A systematic review of power training in team-sport athletes suggests optimal-load and velocity-based methods may be optimal for sessions with less time under tension and shorter session times while maximizing power and velocity.

evidence.excerpt: abilities, thus utilising methods such as OPL and VBT may be optimal for sessions with less TUT, shorter session times, whilst maximising power and velocity throughout.

claims.text: The same review notes that in many team sports recovery may be hindered for up to 72 hours or more after a match, and that weekly technical-tactical and physical training volume may make maintaining power and speed difficult.

evidence.excerpt: in many team-sports, recovery may be hindered for up to 72 h (Doeven et al., 2018) or more (McLean et al., 2010) following a match, and weekly concurrent technical-tactical and physical training volume may pose a problem for coaches wishing to maintain power- and speed-related

claims.text: The review describes mixed training as using relatively lighter loads at higher velocities, which the authors suggest may be beneficial in in-season periods where velocity-specific adaptations matter.

evidence.excerpt: is also characterised by relatively lighter loads moved at higher velocities which may be beneficial in crucial in-season periods where velocity-specific adaptations are key for success in competition.

claims.text: In interviews with 12 applied practitioners across a range of sports, reported strategies for scheduling challenges included micro-dosing the resistance training stimulus and using isometric exercise during fixture congestion.

evidence.excerpt: Twelve practitioners (one physiotherapist and eleven strength and conditioning [S&C] coaches including one dual accredited S&C coach and physiotherapist) working in a range of sporting disciplines were interviewed
strategies to deal with such challenges such as micro-dosing of the resistance training stimulus, utilisation of isometric exercise during ﬁxture congestion periods.

claims.text: In 18 elite football players measured after 3 matches, reductions in the countermovement jump flight time to contraction time ratio persisted later than changes in jump height, and the authors judged it the more sensitive recovery measure.

evidence.excerpt: were measured in 18 elite football players before (27, 1 h) and after (0.5, 18, 42, 66, 90 h) 3 consecutive matches.
Although jump height was reduced immediately postmatch, FT:CT provided a more sensitive measure of recovery.

assumptions: The session is the last structured strength-and-power exposure before competition and sits alongside, not in place of, normal sport practice.
Athletes are familiar with the exercises used, so no novel or unaccustomed loading is introduced in this window.
Readiness was not defined by a specific test, so jump and velocity measures were treated as reasonable proxies.
coverageGaps: No study testing strength-and-power session content or dose 24 to 48 hours before competition with competition-day readiness or performance as the outcome.
No evidence on how long residual fatigue lasts after low-volume, cluster-structured, or velocity-based sessions.
No collegiate multi-sport or female athlete data on pre-competition session dosing.
No source tests a strength-and-power session placed 48 hours before competition or measures next-day competition performance.

A controlled study comparing low-volume strength-and-power sessions 24 to 48 hours before competition, with readiness or performance measured on competition day, would allow a conditional recommendation.
This brief informs professional judgment. It does not prescribe a session, clear an athlete, or set department policy.
The evidence assumes healthy athletes. Any athlete with a medical restriction or new symptom should be handled by the treating clinicians, not by this brief.
